subject: chemistry
title: Properties and Particle Pictures
welcome_lead: Why can you squash a gas but not a brick? Particle pictures hold the answer.
meta_desc: Compare properties of solids, liquids and gases through particle arrangements in this KS3 chemistry adventure.
final_note: You can now explain real-world behaviour using particle diagrams.

Ability to move and change shape; liquids and gases flow.

walkthroughs.body_html: Most solids are denser than liquids because the particles are packed closer. Gases are usually the least dense because their particles are spread far apart.
Solids and liquids cannot be compressed much because their particles are already touching. Gases can be compressed a lot because there is plenty of empty space between particles.

Liquids and gases both flow because their particles can move past each other. Solids do not flow because particles are locked in place.

More movement means more flow.

mcqs.q: Why can gases be compressed easily?
options: There is empty space between gas particles
Gas particles are sticky
Gas particles are heavy
Gases are cold

mcqs.q: Which state is usually the least dense?
options: Solid
Liquid
Gas
All the same

mcqs.q: Why does the colour of a transition metal complex change when ligands are exchanged?
options: The colour changes because the new ligand is itself coloured.
Different ligands cause different amounts of d-orbital splitting, so different wavelengths of light are absorbed.
The colour changes because the metal ion itself changes oxidation state.
Entropy measures how much energy a system contains in total.

mcqs.q: How is a dynamic equilibrium different from a static one?
options: Entropy measures how much energy a system contains in total.
Dynamic and static equilibria are the same thing because both show constant macroscopic properties.
A dynamic equilibrium means the system is still changing visibly.
In a dynamic equilibrium, forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates; in a static equilibrium, nothing is happening at the particle level.

mcqs.q: What does an increase in entropy of a system correspond to?
options: Entropy is just a measure of how messy a system looks visually.
An increase in the number of ways energy and particles can be arranged — typically a more dispersed/'disordered' state.
Entropy measures how much energy a system contains in total.
The colour changes because the new ligand is itself coloured.
